page: Amazon Web Services dl2q.24xlarge is an accelerated computing instance engineered primarily for high-density deep learning inference workloads. Running on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, the host system features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor operating at 2.5 GHz. The CPU subsystem provides 48 physical cores and 96 dedicated vCPUs with hyperthreading enabled, paired with 35 MB of L3 cache and support for AVX-512 vector extensions including VNNI. System memory comprises 768.0 GB of DDR4 RAM running at 3 GHz, delivering an allocation of 8.0 GB per vCPU.

Hardware acceleration is supplied by eight Qualcomm Cloud AI100 inference accelerators, offering a combined 125 GB of total accelerator VRAM. Networking capabilities feature a baseline network bandwidth of 100 Gbps, ensuring sufficient throughput for distributed inference pipelines, data ingestion, and microservice traffic. The instance does not include bundled local storage, requiring persistent workloads to utilize external Amazon EBS or network-attached storage solutions.

Benchmark evaluations highlight the distinction between single-threaded and highly parallel processing capabilities. Multi-core performance is robust, with stress-ng multi-core testing scoring 81,310.77 and PassMark CPU reaching 55,760.63, both placing in the top 25%. Cached memory read throughput reaches 4,504.08 GB/sec, while uncached large-block reads register at 220.46 GB/sec. Static web serving throughput reaches 45.89 GB/sec and Redis SET performance registers 75.32 million operations per second. Conversely, single-core execution is modest, reflected by a stress-ng single-core score of 1,370.79 in the bottom 25% and a Geekbench single-core score of 1,257.0.

The primary operational tradeoff of dl2q.24xlarge is its optimization around parallel throughput and specialized Qualcomm ASIC acceleration rather than raw per-core clock speed. Combined with the absence of integrated NVMe storage, this configuration is purpose-built for scale-out deep learning model inference, computer vision, natural language processing deployments, and data-heavy microservices capable of leveraging dedicated accelerator hardware.
